key_insight: An octopus-inspired soft arm uses distributed optoelectronic mechanosensors embedded in suction cups to detect contact forces and locally infer object position, enabling peripheral (edge) control for autonomous underwater grasping.
problem_solved: How to achieve robust, real-time underwater grasping with a soft manipulator despite limited central sensing bandwidth and complex, variable contact interactions.
method: Embed optoelectronic mechanosensors into each suction cup to measure local contact forces and deformations.
Use distributed/ peripheral processing to translate local sensor signals into contact/contact-point and object-position estimates at the sensor or arm segment level.
Integrate the local estimates into a decentralized control scheme for the soft arm to coordinate suction, closing, and conformal grasping without heavy central computation.
impact: Demonstrates a scalable, bioinspired route to tactile-rich, low-latency grasping by shifting perception and some inference to the edge—useful for AI/ML workflows that need compact, distributed sensing and reduced centralized data/compute for real-world robotic deployments.
visual_elements: Annotated illustration of the soft arm highlighting sensorized suction cups and edge-processing nodes

paper_title: Peripheral control enabled by distributed sensing in an octopus-inspired soft robotic arm for autonomous underwater grasping
paper_authors: Emanuela Del Dottore, Romina Adhami, Ebrahim Shahabi, Emanuele Solfiti, Michele Martini
